primary_text_note: In copyright (Kelman 2011). Verified against LitCharts and GradeSaver chapter summaries, character analyses and quotation pages, SuperSummary, BookBrowse, published Kelman interviews, and specs/aqa/english-literature-8702-8702.md for every exam claim.

findings.claim: All 42 practice questions are typed “30+4 marks — Shakespeare Essay”.
findings.truth: Pigeon English is an AQA 8702 Paper 2 Section A modern prose set text. The question is a modern-text essay, one from a choice of two, no printed extract, closed book. Relabel to “30+4 marks — Modern Text Essay” (the 30+4 marks are right).
findings.evidence: specs/aqa/english-literature-8702-8702.md §3.2.1 lists Stephen Kelman, Pigeon English under Prose; §2 'Paper 2: Modern texts and poetry ... Section A Modern texts: students will answer one essay question from a choice of two'. Same relabel precedent as anita-and-me, dna, a-taste-of-honey.

findings.field: content_html, conclusion_html, exam_tip_html, knowledge_checks, flashcard_questions, glossary_terms, practice_questions
findings.claim: The pigeon-narrator is taught throughout as cold and indifferent: “detached, observational, and almost predatory”; “the pigeon observes Harri’s blood on the ground ... It does not mourn. It does not understand.”; “the reader is left with a cold, inhuman gaze”; “The pigeon’s indifference mirrors society’s indifference”. Lesson 4 KC[1] and lesson 5 KC[1] both mark that description as the CORRECT answer.
findings.truth: The pigeon is a guardian-angel second narrator. Its interludes are calm, adult and philosophical, and it watches over Harri with affection. At the end it does not observe his blood from a distance — it stays with the dying Harri and comforts him: “Don’t worry, you’ll be going home soon. When it’s time to go I’ll show you the way.”, “I’m sorry if it hurts. It won’t be long now.”, “There’s nothing to be scared of.” It grieves (“I do know the shape of a mother’s grief”). The valid thematic point is helplessness, not indifference: the pigeon understands everything and still cannot intervene.
findings.evidence: LitCharts July summary (pigeon assures Harri he is 'going home soon', promises to tell Agnes a story, 'the freeing of the star') https://www.litcharts.com/lit/pigeon-english/july ; GradeSaver July: 'his pigeon appears to comfort him and show him to the afterlife' https://www.gradesaver.com/pigeon-english/study-guide/summary-july ; GradeSaver character list: 'guardian angel figure ... protective, almost mystical tone' https://www.gradesaver.com/pigeon-english/study-guide/character-list ; SuperSummary: 'functions like a guardian angel ... a more somber, adult-like viewpoint'.

findings.field: description, content_html, conclusion_html, exam_tip_html, knowledge_checks, flashcard_questions, glossary_terms, practice_questions
findings.claim: Dean is taught as the streetwise friend who drifts into the Dell Farm Crew — “Dean starts running errands, then carrying things, then being present when violence happens”; lesson 6 gives him a whole character section on that arc; lesson 2 KC[1] marks “Harri’s best friend who is drawn towards the Dell Farm Crew” as the correct answer.
findings.truth: Dean is Harri’s best friend from SCHOOL: brainy, obsessed with CSI, the partner in the detective game, and a TARGET of the Dell Farm Crew (mugged, called 'pussy boys'). He never joins them. The boy who drifts into criminality is JORDAN — Harri’s friend outside school, expelled, who leads Harri into vandalism, steals for the Dell Farm Crew in return for cigarettes and protection, carries the 'war knife', scratches DEAD on the Opokus’ door and finally kills Harri. Lesson 5 already names Jordan correctly, so the unit contradicts itself.
findings.evidence: GradeSaver character list: Dean 'Harri’s school best friend who enjoys detective and crime shows ... frequently targeted by the Dell Farm Crew for his red hair and mugged for money'; Jordan 'becomes deeply involved with criminality. After expulsion he steals for the Dell Farm Crew in exchange for cigarettes and protection, eventually murdering Harri himself.' https://www.gradesaver.com/pigeon-english/study-guide/character-list ; LitCharts character list: Dean 'Harri’s best friend from school ... inspired by Dean’s love of the CSI television show'; Jordan 'has been expelled from school'. https://www.litcharts.com/lit/pigeon-english/characters

findings.claim: “He believes in right and wrong, wants justice for the murdered boy, and resists the pressure to join the Dell Farm Crew”, and the glossary: his moral compass “makes him refuse to join the gang”.
findings.truth: Harri does not refuse. X-Fire sets him an initiation — set off the fire alarm — and Harri attempts it. He hits the alarm but the glass does not break, and he runs away fearing the Crew are now his enemies. Whether his hands were 'too soft' or he did not truly want to do it is left open, and that ambiguity is the AO2 point.
findings.evidence: LitCharts April summary / X-Fire character analysis: X-Fire dares Harri to pull the fire alarm to prove he has 'got what it takes'; Harri hits it, the glass does not break, and he runs. https://www.litcharts.com/lit/pigeon-english/april

findings.claim: The <dfn> on the word “redemptive” carries data-def “A word or image referring to something well-known, such as a real event, person, or text. Kelman’s allusion to Damilola Taylor’s murder gives the novel political urgency.”
findings.truth: That is the definition of ALLUSION, not 'redemptive'. The lesson’s own glossary_terms entry for 'redemptive' already reads 'Something that offers hope, salvation, or compensation for suffering.' The tooltip a student sees contradicts the glossary.

findings.claim: The memorisation list glosses “hutious” as “his invented superlative”, and the flashcard repeats “'Hutious' (his superlative)”.
findings.truth: Hutious means scary or frightening — it is not a superlative, and it is Ghanaian slang rather than Harri’s invention. Lessons 2 and 6 define it correctly, so lesson 7 contradicts the rest of the unit. A student who writes that hutious is Harri’s word for 'brilliant' loses the AO2 point.
findings.evidence: Ghanaian slang glossaries and the Kelman interview headlined 'So that’s what hutious means!' (Three Monkeys Online); lessons 2 and 6 of this unit already gloss it as scary/frightening.

findings.claim: Harri “creates his own ranking system” and uses “his own invented words (‘hutious’ ... ‘bo-styles’ ... ‘asweh’)”; flashcards ask for “Harri’s invented slang words”.
findings.truth: Hutious, bo-styles and asweh are Ghanaian slang that Harri brings with him, not coinages. The AO2 point Kelman is actually making is the collision of Ghanaian speech with London playground slang — which is what the same lessons say two sentences earlier.
findings.evidence: Ghanaian slang sources for hutious/asweh; the unit’s own description of Harri’s voice as a mix of Ghanaian English and London slang.

findings.claim: “Kelman has said he wanted to ‘give a voice to the voiceless’” — presented as a direct authorial quotation, then set as a KC fill answer (KC[3], answer 'voice') and a flashcard answer ('What stated authorial purpose did Kelman give for the novel?').
findings.truth: I could not find this phrase in any Kelman interview. What IS documented: Kelman describes the novel as 'a tribute to' Damilola Taylor; in interview he says 'All I can do is try to portray my characters as realistically as I can', and describes watching boys on his own estate and asking 'which one of these kids is going to fall in this way or get out of this environment to do good?'. Options: (a) drop the quotation marks and the attribution, keeping the idea as paraphrase; (b) replace the KC and flashcard with the sourced 'tribute to Damilola Taylor' purpose. I recommend (b) — it is verifiable and it is the AO3 point students actually need.
findings.evidence: Searched Kelman interviews (Three Monkeys Online, Writers & Artists, BookPage) and LitCharts/GradeSaver context pages; no instance of 'a voice to the voiceless'. LitCharts context: Kelman wrote Pigeon English as 'a tribute to' Damilola Taylor.

findings.claim: “He hears gunshots and thinks they are fireworks” — given as the worked example of Harri misreading danger, and set as a flashcard answer ('Give an example of Harri misreading danger on the estate.').
findings.truth: I could not verify this moment in the novel from any summary, quotation collection or study guide. Verified alternatives exist and are better evidenced: Harri names a fancy water pistol when a streetwise friend asks his favourite gun; Harri treats the murder investigation as a CSI game; Harri watches the Dell Farm Crew burn the playground and describes the fire as 'lovely and sleepy'. Recommend swapping the fireworks example for the water-pistol answer in both places, unless someone with the text can confirm it.
findings.evidence: Searched BookBrowse, SuperSummary, GradeSaver, LitCharts and the quotation collections; the water-pistol moment appears, the fireworks moment does not.

findings.claim: “Harri is stabbed in the stairwell by Jordan”, and the key fact “Harri is killed by Jordan in the stairwell — not the Dell Farm Crew collectively”, stated as settled fact in a KC and a flashcard.
findings.truth: The detail is right in substance (stairwell, war knife, the remote-control-car quarrel, the DEAD scratched on the door) and Jordan is the mainstream reading. But Kelman never names the attacker, and the guides split: GradeSaver says 'an unnamed killer — likely Jordan', LitCharts’ July summary reads it as Killa or another Dell Farm Crew member taking revenge before Harri can talk to the police. Both readings earn marks. Recommend softening to 'the novel never names the attacker; the evidence points to Jordan' in the content and the flashcard, and leaving the KC option as the strongest reading.
findings.evidence: GradeSaver July summary: 'An unnamed killer—likely Jordan—stabs Harri in the apartment stairwell' https://www.gradesaver.com/pigeon-english/study-guide/summary-july ; LitCharts July summary attributes it to an unnamed boy, presumably Killa or another Crew member.

findings.claim: “the dispute over Auntie Sonia’s remote-control car”.
findings.truth: The car is Harri’s — a present from Auntie Sonia. Harri shows it off to Jordan and refuses him a turn. Not worth an edit; the fact behind it is right.
findings.evidence: GradeSaver summary: Auntie Sonia gives Harri a remote control car; Harri brings it to Jordan’s flat and refuses him a go.

findings.claim: The glossary term “pigeon” is defined as “An object, character, or image that represents a larger idea or concept” — the definition of 'symbol'.
findings.truth: Same class of slip as F5, but the sentence that follows does explain the pigeon, so a student is not misled. Left alone.

findings.claim: Mamma is compared to “Mrs Johnstone in Blood Brothers”.
findings.truth: Accurate as an analogy, but AQA Paper 2 Section A is a single-text closed-book essay and students who have not studied Blood Brothers cannot use it. Not wrong, so not edited — flagged only in case the house style bars cross-text comparisons in a set-text lesson.
findings.evidence: spec 8702 §2: 'students will answer one essay question ... on their studied modern prose or drama text'.

summary: Two systematic errors run through the unit. The pigeon-narrator is taught as cold and indifferent when it is in fact a guardian who stays with the dying Harri and comforts him, and two knowledge checks mark that false description as the correct answer (L4, L5, L7). Dean is given Jordan’s arc — the drift into the Dell Farm Crew — across lessons 2, 4 and 6, contradicting lesson 5, which names Jordan as the killer correctly. Plus the fleet-wide “Shakespeare Essay” label on all 42 practice questions, a mis-stated gang initiation, a swapped glossary tooltip and two slips about Harri’s Ghanaian slang. The AO claims added on 30 Aug are correct: AO1 12 / AO2 12 / AO3 6 + 4 SPaG, 30 marks, no printed extract, closed book, all match the spec. Lesson 3 carries only the shared practice-question relabel.
